slides.title: What is a problem?
slides.text: A problem is something that needs fixing. Your block tower falling down is a problem.

slides.title: Try a different way
slides.text: If one way does not work, try a new way. Use a wide block instead of a thin one.

slides.title: Mistakes are okay
slides.text: It is okay to make mistakes. Your tower fell down three times, and that is okay too.

slides.title: Asking for help is smart
slides.text: If you feel stuck, ask for help. A grown-up or a friend can help you.

slides.title: Small steps first
slides.text: A messy room feels big. Doing one small step at a time makes it easy.

slides.title: Celebrate figuring it out
slides.text: When you solve a problem, feel proud! You worked hard to fix it.

slides.title: A broken toy
slides.text: A toy can break. You can try to fix it, or ask a grown-up to help you.

slides.title: Take a breath
slides.text: Feeling upset is okay. Take a deep breath, then try again.

slides.title: Going slow helps
slides.text: Going slow can help you. Rushing can cause more mistakes.

slides.title: Practice makes it easier
slides.text: The more you practice, the easier it gets. Tying your shoes gets easier every time you try.

quiz.question: What is a "problem"?
choices: Something that needs fixing
Something that is already perfect
quiz.explanation: A problem is something that needs fixing, like a puzzle piece that won't fit. Noticing it is the first step.

quiz.question: Your tower keeps falling. What should you try?
choices: A different way
Nothing at all
quiz.explanation: A new way can work better. Try a wide block instead of a thin one.

quiz.question: Is it okay to make mistakes?
choices: Yes, mistakes are okay
No, mistakes are bad
quiz.explanation: Mistakes help you learn. Falling three times before your tower stood is just part of trying.

quiz.question: You feel stuck. What can you do?
choices: Ask for help
Never ask anyone
quiz.explanation: Asking for help is smart, not weak. A grown-up or friend can show you a trick you hadn't thought of.

quiz.question: How can a messy room feel less big?
choices: Do one small step at a time
Try to do it all at once
quiz.explanation: A messy room feels less scary in small steps. Pick up just the blocks first, then the books next.

quiz.question: You finally fix your tower. What should you do?
choices: Feel nothing at all
Feel proud of yourself
quiz.explanation: Solving a problem feels great, like your tower finally standing tall. Feeling proud is a fair reward for trying hard.

quiz.question: Your toy breaks. What can you do?
choices: Try to fix it or ask for help
Throw it away right away
quiz.explanation: A broken toy isn't the end. Try fixing it, like taping a torn stuffed bear, or ask a grown-up.

quiz.question: You feel upset about a problem. What should you do first?
choices: Yell and stomp
Take a deep breath
quiz.explanation: Feeling upset about a problem is normal. Taking a deep breath first helps you calm down before you try again.

quiz.question: Why can going slow help you?
choices: It helps you make fewer mistakes
It always wastes time
quiz.explanation: Going slow helps you be careful, like carrying a full cup without spilling it. Rushing often leads to more mistakes.

quiz.question: Why does practice help with problems?
choices: Practice never changes anything
It makes problems easier over time
quiz.explanation: Practice makes hard things easier, like tying your shoes. The more times you try, the better you get.

slides.title: Sorting and matching
slides.text: Matching socks into pairs is fun practice. It helps you notice what goes together.

slides.title: One step at a time
slides.text: You do not have to solve it all at once. Just do the next small step.

slides.title: Think of a few ideas
slides.text: Try to think of two or three ideas. Then pick the best one to try.

slides.title: What did you learn?
slides.text: After a mistake, think about what happened. It can help you do better next time.

slides.title: Keep trying
slides.text: Do not give up too fast. Try one more time before you stop.

slides.title: Look closely first
slides.text: Look closely before you start. Noticing small things can help you solve it.

slides.title: Follow the clues
slides.text: Clues help you solve problems. If your snack is missing, look for crumbs to find out who took it.

slides.title: Think before you act
slides.text: Thinking first helps. Before you grab a tool, think about what you need it for.

slides.title: Ask "why"
slides.text: Asking why helps you understand. Why did the balloon pop? Maybe it touched something sharp.

slides.title: Toy cleanup sort
slides.text: Putting toys into groups, like cars together and blocks together, makes cleanup faster.

quiz.question: What do you practice when you match socks?
choices: Noticing what goes together
Nothing useful
quiz.explanation: Matching socks means finding pairs that look the same. That helps you notice patterns, like sorting red socks together.

quiz.question: Before you try to fix something, what should you do?
choices: Pick the very first idea only
Think of a few ideas first
quiz.explanation: Thinking of a few ideas first helps you pick the best one, like using a stool to reach a shelf.

quiz.question: After a mistake, what is a good question to ask?
choices: What can I learn from this?
Why does this always happen to me?
quiz.explanation: Asking what you can learn helps you do better next time, like holding a cup with two hands after a spill.

quiz.question: Your first try does not work. What should you do?
choices: Try one more time
Give up right away
quiz.explanation: Trying again is how you solve problems. Maybe your next tower will stand up tall.

quiz.question: You cannot find your favorite toy. What should you do first?
choices: Look closely for small clues
Give up looking
quiz.explanation: Looking closely helps you spot small clues. A toy car's wheel peeking out can show you where it rolled.

quiz.question: Your snack is missing. What can crumbs on the floor help you do?
choices: Find out who took it
Nothing, crumbs do not help
quiz.explanation: Crumbs on the floor are a clue, like a trail leading to who ate your cookie. Clues help you solve a mystery.

quiz.question: Before you grab a tool, what should you do?
choices: Grab any tool without thinking
Think about what you need it for
quiz.explanation: Thinking first helps you pick the right tool, like a spoon instead of a fork for soup.

quiz.question: A balloon pops. What is a good question to ask?
choices: Why did that happen?
Nothing, just walk away
quiz.explanation: Asking why helps you understand what happened. Maybe the balloon touched something sharp, like a pointy toy.

quiz.question: How can you clean up toys faster?
choices: Put similar toys into groups
Throw them all in one big pile
quiz.explanation: Putting toys into groups, like all the cars in one bin, makes cleanup much faster.

quiz.question: You do not have to solve a big job all at once. What should you do?
choices: Do the next small step
Try to finish everything right now
quiz.explanation: A big job feels smaller in small steps, like cleaning one shelf before moving to the next.

slides.title: Understanding the real problem
slides.text: Before you try to fix something, figure out what's really wrong. A toy robot might be broken, or it might just need new batteries.

slides.title: Breaking it into smaller parts
slides.text: A big problem is easier to handle when you split it into smaller parts. Instead of "clean the whole garage," try "clear one shelf at a time."

slides.title: Asking good questions
slides.text: Asking the right question can point you straight to a solution. Instead of asking "why is this broken," ask "what changed right before it broke?"

slides.title: Brainstorming ideas
slides.text: Coming up with a few ideas before choosing one usually works better than grabbing the first idea. To reach a high snack, you could use a step stool, ask someone, or use a broom.

slides.title: Looking from a new angle
slides.text: When a problem feels stuck, try looking at it in a totally different way. Imagining how a very organized friend would sort your toys might reveal an idea you missed.

slides.title: Using tools to help
slides.text: The right tool can make a problem much easier to solve, like a ruler, a calculator, or a checklist. Measuring wood with a ruler instead of guessing keeps you from cutting the wrong size.

slides.title: Naming the problem out loud
slides.text: Saying or writing down the problem clearly helps you focus on fixing it. "My science poster looks messy" is a lot clearer than just feeling frustrated and not knowing why.

slides.title: Picturing the goal
slides.text: Imagining exactly what "finished" looks like helps you know which ideas actually move you closer to it. Picture the finished blanket fort before you start grabbing pillows and chairs.

slides.title: Checking your assumptions
slides.text: Sometimes we assume we already know why something's wrong, but checking first can save a lot of wasted effort. A bike chain that slips might not need a whole new chain — check if it's just loose first.

slides.title: One clue at a time
slides.text: Solving a mystery problem, like why the Wi-Fi keeps disconnecting, often means checking one possible cause at a time instead of guessing randomly.

quiz.question: A toy robot won't walk. Why figure out the real problem first?
choices: So you know if it needs batteries or a real repair
It's better to just guess
quiz.explanation: Figuring out the real problem first stops you from wasting effort fixing the wrong thing. Checking the batteries before taking a toy robot apart can save you a lot of extra work.

quiz.question: How can a huge job like cleaning a garage feel easier?
choices: Split it into smaller parts
Try to do it all in one go
quiz.explanation: Splitting a big job into smaller parts makes it far less overwhelming. Instead of "clean the whole garage," try clearing just one shelf, then move to the next.

quiz.question: Instead of asking "why is this broken," what's a better question to ask?
choices: Nothing, one question is as good as another
What changed right before it broke?
quiz.explanation: A sharper question points you straight to the answer instead of leaving you guessing. Asking what changed right before something broke often reveals the real cause faster.

quiz.question: What is "brainstorming"?
choices: Thinking of a few solutions before choosing one
Picking the very first idea you think of
quiz.explanation: Brainstorming means thinking of several ideas, like a stool, help, or a broom, before choosing one. Comparing options usually works better than grabbing the very first idea.

quiz.question: Your toy sorting is stuck. What might help?
choices: Refusing to think about it any differently
Imagining how someone very organized would do it
quiz.explanation: Looking at a stuck problem from a new angle can reveal ideas you'd otherwise miss. Imagining how a super organized friend would sort your toys might show a system you hadn't thought of.

quiz.question: Why measure wood with a ruler instead of guessing?
choices: It helps you avoid cutting the wrong size
Tools never actually help
quiz.explanation: The right tool makes a tricky job easier and more accurate. Measuring wood with a ruler instead of guessing keeps you from cutting a piece the wrong size and wasting material.

quiz.question: Why is "my science poster looks messy" more useful than just feeling frustrated?
choices: It clearly names what actually needs fixing
Feelings and problems are exactly the same thing
quiz.explanation: Naming a problem clearly helps you focus your effort on actually fixing it. Saying "my poster looks messy" points you toward a real fix, while just feeling frustrated does not.

quiz.question: Before building a blanket fort, why picture the finished fort first?
choices: It helps you know which steps actually move you toward it
Picturing things never actually helps you plan
quiz.explanation: Picturing exactly what "finished" looks like helps you know which steps actually move you closer to it. Imagining the finished fort first keeps you from randomly grabbing pillows and chairs.

quiz.question: A bike chain keeps slipping. What should you check before buying a new chain?
choices: Nothing, just replace it right away
Whether the chain is simply loose
quiz.explanation: Checking your assumption first can save time and money before buying something new. A slipping chain might just be loose, not broken, so tightening it could be the whole fix.

quiz.question: Your Wi-Fi keeps disconnecting for an unknown reason. What's a smart approach?
choices: Check one possible cause at a time
Guess randomly and hope something works
quiz.explanation: Checking one possible cause at a time is more reliable than guessing randomly. You might test the router first, then the settings, until you find the real reason it keeps disconnecting.

slides.title: Trial and error
slides.text: Trial and error means trying something, checking if it works, and adjusting when it doesn't. If a step stool isn't tall enough, you try a taller one next.

slides.title: Learning from what didn't work
slides.text: When a solution fails, figuring out why helps you avoid the same mistake later. If a paper airplane keeps nose-diving, a heavy nose is often the reason.

slides.title: Testing your idea first
slides.text: Trying a solution on a small scale first can catch problems early. Testing one paper airplane design before making ten of them saves time and paper.

slides.title: Comparing your solutions
slides.text: When you have more than one solution, think about which is fastest, easiest, or works best. Comparing options helps you pick the smartest one, not just the first one you thought of.

slides.title: Solving problems with others
slides.text: Working with someone else can bring up ideas you wouldn't think of alone. A friend might notice something about balance that you missed while building a tower.

slides.title: Taking a break when stuck
slides.text: Stepping away from a tricky problem for a few minutes can help your brain find a fresh idea. After a short break, you often spot things you missed before.

slides.title: Staying calm when frustrated
slides.text: Feeling frustrated is normal when a problem is hard to solve. Taking a breath and staying calm helps you think more clearly.

slides.title: Bouncing back from a setback
slides.text: Treating a setback as one data point, not the end of the story, keeps you moving forward. Losing the first round of a game can just mean learning the other player's strategy for next time.

slides.title: Knowing when "good enough" is good enough
slides.text: Not every solution has to be perfect. A tent that's a little crooked but still keeps out the rain is a perfectly fine solution for one night of camping.

slides.title: Checking in halfway
slides.text: Partway through a long project, like a big Lego build, stopping to check if you're still on the right track can save you from redoing work later.

quiz.question: A step stool doesn't reach, so you try a taller one. What is this called?
choices: Trial and error
Doing the same failed thing forever
quiz.explanation: Trial and error means trying something, checking if it works, and changing your approach if it doesn't. Trying a taller step stool after a short one fails is a perfect example.

quiz.question: A paper airplane keeps nose-diving because the nose is too heavy. Why does figuring that out help?
choices: It helps you avoid the same mistake next time
It's better to forget about it completely
quiz.explanation: Figuring out why something failed helps you fix it instead of repeating the mistake. Knowing a heavy nose makes a plane nose-dive tells you exactly what to change next time.

quiz.question: Why test one paper airplane design before making ten?
choices: It catches problems early and saves time
Testing first is always a waste of time
quiz.explanation: Testing a small version first catches problems before you've wasted a lot of time or materials. Trying one design before folding ten copies saves both paper and effort.

quiz.question: You have three ways to fix a wobbly table leg. What should you do?
choices: Just pick the first idea you had
Compare which is fastest, easiest, and works best
quiz.explanation: Comparing your options, like which fix is fastest or easiest, helps you choose the smartest solution. Grabbing the very first idea might not actually be the best one.

quiz.question: How can working with a friend help solve a problem?
choices: It can bring up ideas you wouldn't think of alone
It never helps at all
quiz.explanation: Working with a friend brings in a second set of eyes and ideas you might not think of alone. A friend might spot a wobble in your tower's base that you completely missed.

quiz.question: Why might a short break help with a tricky puzzle?
choices: Your brain can come back with a fresh idea
Breaks never help with anything
quiz.explanation: Stepping away from a hard puzzle for a few minutes lets your brain rest and reset. When you come back, you often notice a clue you missed the first time.

quiz.question: You feel frustrated because a problem is hard. What helps?
choices: Getting angrier at the problem
Taking a breath and staying calm
quiz.explanation: Feeling frustrated when a problem is hard is completely normal. Taking a breath and staying calm helps you think clearly instead of getting stuck in the frustration.

quiz.question: You lose the first round of a game. What's the most useful way to think about it?
choices: As a chance to learn the other player's strategy
As proof you should quit the game
quiz.explanation: Treating a lost round as useful information, not a disaster, keeps you moving forward. Losing round one might just mean you now know the other player's strategy for round two.

quiz.question: Your camping tent is a little crooked but keeps out the rain. What should you do?
choices: Accept it — it's a good enough solution for one night
Refuse to camp until it's perfectly straight
quiz.explanation: Not every solution has to be perfect to actually work. A tent that leans a little but still keeps the rain out is good enough for one night of camping.

quiz.question: Partway through a big Lego build, why pause to check your progress?
choices: It can save you from redoing work later
Checking partway through never matters
quiz.explanation: Pausing partway through a big project to check your progress can catch a mistake early. Stopping to compare with the instructions can save you from tearing it apart later.

slides.title: Breaking big problems into small ones
slides.text: A big, overwhelming problem becomes much more manageable once it's broken into smaller, clearer pieces you can tackle one at a time. For example, "plan an entire birthday party" feels huge, but breaking it into "pick a date," "make a guest list," "choose food," and "plan activities" turns it into four manageable tasks instead of one overwhelming one.

slides.title: Weighing pros and cons
slides.text: When you have more than one possible solution, listing the good and bad points of each helps you choose more wisely than just going with a gut feeling. For example, choosing between joining the soccer team or the debate club might come down to listing what you'd gain and give up with each — time commitment, what you'd learn, who you'd meet — rather than just picking whichever sounds more fun in the moment.

slides.title: Planning the steps
slides.text: Once you've picked a solution, mapping out the order of steps needed to actually do it makes the plan far more likely to succeed. For example, if you decide to organize a class fundraiser, mapping out the order — get permission first, then plan the activity, then advertise it, then run it — keeps you from accidentally skipping something important like getting permission.

slides.title: Organizing your approach
slides.text: Writing down your plan, or listing the steps in order, helps you stay on track and notice quickly if something's been missed. For example, writing out "1) buy supplies, 2) make the product, 3) set up the table, 4) advertise" as an actual checklist makes it obvious if you forgot a step, instead of only realizing it halfway through.

slides.title: Generating multiple solutions
slides.text: Before settling on an approach, it's worth generating several different possible solutions rather than running with the first one that comes to mind. For example, if your school project needs a creative presentation, brainstorming options like a poster, a short video, a model, or a skit — before picking one — usually leads to a stronger final choice than committing to your very first idea.

slides.title: Setting a realistic deadline
slides.text: When planning the steps of a project, giving each step a rough deadline instead of a vague "someday" keeps a big task, like a science fair board, from turning into a last-minute scramble. For example, giving yourself Monday for research, Wednesday for the write-up, and Friday for the display keeps the whole project from piling up the night before it's due.

slides.title: Must-haves vs. nice-to-haves
slides.text: When time is limited, separating what a solution absolutely needs from what would just be a nice bonus helps you spend your effort wisely. For example, for a class presentation, clearly explaining the topic is a must-have, while fancy slide animations are a nice-to-have that can wait if time runs short.

slides.title: Choosing the right order
slides.text: Some steps have to happen before others, and planning the correct order prevents wasted, redo-it-all work. For example, you can't reasonably decorate a cake before you bake it — figuring out the right order first saves you from starting over.

slides.title: Setting a clear goal before planning
slides.text: Before mapping out steps, it helps to state exactly what "done" looks like, since a fuzzy goal makes it hard to plan clear steps toward it. For example, "raise $50 for the animal shelter" gives you a clear target to plan around, while "do a fundraiser" leaves you guessing what success even means.

slides.title: Getting a second opinion on your plan
slides.text: Before starting, showing your plan to someone else can catch a problem you missed, since it's easy to overlook gaps in your own plan. For example, a friend might notice your group project plan doesn't account for a teammate being absent one day, something you hadn't thought to plan around.

quiz.question: Why break "plan an entire birthday party" into smaller pieces like date, guest list, and food?
choices: It becomes far more manageable to tackle one piece at a time
It makes the problem more confusing
quiz.explanation: A goal like "plan an entire birthday party" feels huge as one giant task. Breaking it into picking a date, making a guest list, and choosing food turns it into four clear jobs you can actually start today.

quiz.question: What does "weighing pros and cons" help you do when choosing between soccer and debate club?
choices: Choose more wisely between multiple solutions
Avoid ever making a decision
quiz.explanation: Listing the good and bad points of each option, like time commitment or who you'd meet, pushes you past your first gut reaction. That usually leads to a wiser choice than just picking whatever sounds fun in the moment.

quiz.question: You decide to organize a class fundraiser. What should you do right after picking that solution?
choices: Just start advertising with no plan
Map out the order of steps, like getting permission first
quiz.explanation: Once you've chosen a solution, mapping out the order of steps keeps you from missing something important. Getting permission before advertising matters — skip that step and the whole plan could get shut down.

quiz.question: How does writing "1) buy supplies, 2) make the product, 3) set up, 4) advertise" as a checklist help?
choices: It helps you stay on track and notice missed steps
Writing it down never actually helps
quiz.explanation: Writing out steps as an actual checklist makes it obvious right away if something got skipped. Without it, you might not realize you forgot a step until you're already halfway through.

quiz.question: You're picking how to present a school project. What should you do before choosing?
choices: Brainstorm several different options first
Commit to the very first idea you think of
quiz.explanation: Generating several options — a poster, a video, a model, a skit — before choosing gives you more to compare than grabbing whatever idea popped into your head first. The extra ideas usually push you toward a stronger choice.

quiz.question: Why give each step of a science fair project its own rough deadline instead of a vague "someday"?
choices: Deadlines only add unnecessary pressure
It keeps the project from becoming a last-minute scramble
quiz.explanation: Giving each step its own rough deadline, like research on Monday and writeup on Wednesday, spreads the work out evenly. Without deadlines, a project can easily pile up into one stressful night before it's due.

quiz.question: For a class presentation, why is clearly explaining the topic a "must-have" while fancy slide animations are a "nice-to-have"?
choices: Animations always matter more than explaining the topic clearly
It helps you spend limited time on what actually matters most
quiz.explanation: Separating what a solution truly needs from what's just a bonus helps you spend limited time wisely. Explaining the topic clearly is a must-have, while animations are a nice-to-have you can skip if time runs short.

quiz.question: Why can't you reasonably decorate a cake before you bake it?
choices: Some steps have to happen before others in the right order
Order never actually matters when solving a problem
quiz.explanation: Some steps depend on earlier ones being finished first, so the right order matters as much as the steps themselves. You can't decorate a cake before it's baked without starting the whole thing over.

quiz.question: Why is "raise $50 for the animal shelter" a better goal than "do a fundraiser"?
choices: It's vague on purpose, which is always better
It gives you a clear target to plan concrete steps around
quiz.explanation: A specific goal, like raising $50, gives you a clear target to measure your plan against. A vague goal like "do a fundraiser" leaves you guessing what success even means, making it harder to plan real steps.

quiz.question: Why show your group project plan to a friend before starting?
choices: They might catch a gap you overlooked, like a teammate's absence
Other people's opinions are never useful before starting
quiz.explanation: It's easy to overlook gaps in your own plan simply because you're too close to it. A friend might catch something you missed, like not accounting for a teammate being absent one day.

slides.title: Sticking with it through frustration
slides.text: Problem solving often gets frustrating before it gets easier. Pushing through that middle, frustrating part is often exactly what separates success from giving up. For example, learning a new skateboard trick often involves falling repeatedly and feeling frustrated right before you finally land it — that frustrating middle stretch is completely normal, not a sign to quit.

slides.title: Adjusting the plan
slides.text: A good plan isn't set in stone — if something isn't working partway through, adjusting the plan is smarter than stubbornly sticking with a failing approach. For example, if your plan to raise money by selling baked goods isn't attracting buyers, switching to selling something else, or changing your location, is smarter than stubbornly sticking with a plan that clearly isn't working.

slides.title: Focusing on what you can control
slides.text: Some parts of a problem are out of your control. Focusing your energy on the parts you can actually influence tends to be far more productive. For example, you can't control whether it rains on the day of your outdoor event, but you can control having a backup indoor plan ready — focusing your energy there is far more useful than worrying about the weather.

slides.title: Testing your solution safely
slides.text: Before rolling out a solution fully, trying it on a small scale first — like testing one part of a plan — helps catch problems before they get big. For example, before committing to selling 100 friendship bracelets at a big school fair, testing the idea by selling just 5 to classmates first can reveal pricing or design problems while the stakes are still small.

slides.title: Pacing yourself on a long problem
slides.text: Big problems that stretch over days or weeks, like training for a tryout, go better when you pace your effort evenly instead of burning out in the first two days. For example, spreading practice across the two weeks leading up to a tryout works better than cramming every drill into the first weekend and having nothing left by the actual tryout.

slides.title: Recognizing when you're truly stuck
slides.text: There's a difference between a task simply being hard and an approach genuinely not working at all, and noticing which one you're in tells you whether to push harder or change direction completely. For example, struggling to memorize lines for a play is normal and just needs more practice, but reciting them the exact same way for a week with zero improvement might mean trying a different memorization method instead.

slides.title: Making a backup plan
slides.text: Before an important moment, like a class debate, having a backup plan ready for something going wrong keeps one small hiccup from derailing the whole thing. For example, if your debate partner might be absent that day, preparing to cover both sides yourself means one absence doesn't sink the whole plan.

slides.title: Managing frustration in the moment
slides.text: When frustration spikes in the middle of a task, pausing instead of forcing the same failing move harder usually solves it faster. For example, yanking harder on a stuck bike lock rarely helps, but pausing to recheck the combination often reveals a simple mistake, like one wrong number.

slides.title: Noticing small wins along the way
slides.text: Long problems can feel discouraging if you only judge yourself by the final result, so noticing small pieces of progress along the way helps keep you motivated. For example, finally landing one new dance move correctly, even before mastering the whole routine, is real progress worth noticing.

slides.title: Knowing when to change your entire approach
slides.text: Sometimes a small tweak isn't enough, and the smarter move is scrapping the current approach and starting fresh rather than patching something fundamentally flawed. For example, if a group project's poster layout is confusing no matter how it's tweaked, redesigning the whole layout from scratch can be faster than endlessly patching a flawed one.

quiz.question: Learning a new skateboard trick involves falling repeatedly right before landing it. Why does frustration often show up during problem solving?
choices: It's a normal part of the process, and pushing through it often leads to success
It means you should give up immediately
quiz.explanation: Frustration often shows up right in the middle of learning something hard, before it actually clicks. Falling repeatedly while learning a new skateboard trick is normal, not a sign that you should quit.

quiz.question: Your bake sale plan isn't attracting buyers. What's the smart move?
choices: Adjust the plan
Stubbornly keep doing the same failing thing forever
quiz.explanation: A good plan isn't set in stone — if part of it isn't working, changing it beats stubbornly repeating the same approach. Switching products or moving to a busier spot makes more sense than doing the exact same thing again.

quiz.question: You can't control the weather for your outdoor event, but you can prepare a backup indoor plan. Why focus there?
choices: Your energy is more productive there than on things you can't influence
Nothing is ever within your control
quiz.explanation: Worrying about the weather wastes energy you can't use to change anything. Focusing instead on a solid backup indoor plan is something you actually can control, which makes that effort far more productive.

quiz.question: Why test selling 5 bracelets to classmates before committing to 100 at a big fair?
choices: It helps catch problems before they get big
Testing small scale never reveals anything useful
quiz.explanation: Testing an idea on a small scale can reveal pricing or design problems while very little is at stake. Finding those issues early beats discovering them after committing to selling 100 at a big fair.

quiz.question: Why spread tryout practice evenly across two weeks instead of cramming it all into the first weekend?
choices: Cramming everything early always works better
It keeps you from burning out before the actual tryout
quiz.explanation: Pacing your practice evenly keeps your energy and motivation lasting until the actual tryout. Cramming every drill into the first weekend can leave you exhausted and under-practiced by the day that counts.

quiz.question: You've recited play lines the exact same way for a week with zero improvement. What might that mean?
choices: It might be worth trying a different memorization method
It definitely just needs a little more of the exact same practice
quiz.explanation: Struggling at first with something hard is normal and usually just needs more practice. But reciting lines the same failing way for a week with zero improvement is a sign the method itself isn't working.

quiz.question: Your debate partner might be absent on debate day. What's a smart move beforehand?
choices: Assume it won't happen and make no backup plan
Prepare to cover both sides yourself just in case
quiz.explanation: A backup plan ready for something going wrong keeps one small hiccup from wrecking the whole thing. Preparing to cover both sides yourself means the debate can still go smoothly even if your partner can't make it.

quiz.question: A bike lock is stuck. What usually helps more than yanking on it harder?
choices: Pausing to recheck the combination
Pulling even harder until it gives up
quiz.explanation: When frustration spikes, forcing the same failing move harder rarely helps and can make things worse. Pausing to recheck the combination usually reveals a simple mistake, like one wrong number, much faster.

quiz.question: Why notice finally landing one new dance move, even before mastering the whole routine?
choices: Small wins along the way help keep you motivated
Only the fully finished result ever counts as progress
quiz.explanation: Long problems can feel discouraging if you only judge yourself by the final result. Landing one new dance move correctly is real progress worth celebrating even before you've mastered the whole routine.

quiz.question: A group project's poster layout stays confusing no matter how it's tweaked. What's the smarter move?
choices: Keep patching the same flawed layout forever
Redesign the whole layout from scratch
quiz.explanation: Sometimes small tweaks aren't enough to fix something fundamentally flawed, and continuing to patch it just wastes time. Redesigning a confusing layout from scratch is often faster than endlessly fiddling with a broken one.

slides.title: Checking if it actually worked
slides.text: After trying a solution, honestly checking whether it actually solved the problem — not just whether it felt good to try — is an important last step. For example, if your new study method felt productive but your next test score didn't actually improve, honestly noticing that mismatch matters more than how the studying felt in the moment.

slides.title: Help isn't giving up
slides.text: Reaching out for help after genuinely trying on your own is a sign of good judgment, not a failure to solve the problem yourself. For example, if you've spent real effort troubleshooting a coding project and you're still stuck, asking a teacher or looking up a forum post written by someone who solved the same issue is a smart, efficient next step.

slides.title: Reflecting on mistakes
slides.text: Looking back at what went wrong after a mistake, and being specific about it, teaches you far more than just feeling bad about it. For example, if a group project fell behind schedule, figuring out exactly where it slipped — was it unclear roles, or a missed deadline — helps you avoid the same slip on the next project.

slides.title: Managing your time
slides.text: Solving a problem well often means managing how much time you spend on each part, instead of getting stuck perfecting one piece while ignoring the rest. For example, if you have a week to prepare for a debate, setting rough time limits for research, practice, and rebuttals keeps you from spending five days on research and only one day practicing.

slides.title: Measuring success the right way
slides.text: Deciding upfront what "success" will look like makes it much easier to honestly judge afterward whether a solution actually worked. For example, deciding before a school clean-up event that success means "at least 20 bags of trash collected" gives you an honest way to measure it afterward, instead of just guessing based on how the day felt.

slides.title: Trying again with a change
slides.text: If a first attempt falls short, trying again with one specific, intentional change is far more useful than simply repeating the exact same approach and hoping for a different result. For example, if a lemonade stand made little money on a slow street corner, moving to a busier corner next time is a specific change worth testing, rather than just setting up in the same spot again.

slides.title: Keeping a simple problem-solving journal
slides.text: Jotting a quick note about what worked and what didn't right after solving something builds a habit of noticing patterns over time. For example, writing "starting my homework right after school works better than after dinner" after just a few tries can turn into a genuinely useful personal rule.

slides.title: Turning a mistake into a rule for next time
slides.text: Turning a specific mistake into a concrete rule makes the lesson much more likely to actually stick than just feeling bad about it. For example, after forgetting to charge a laptop before a presentation, the rule "charge devices the night before, every time" is far more useful than simply resolving to "be more careful."

slides.title: Separating effort from outcome
slides.text: Sometimes you do everything right and still don't get the result you wanted, and recognizing that your effort was genuinely solid, separate from the outcome, matters. For example, trying out for a team with real preparation and still not making the roster doesn't mean the preparation was wasted — the outcome and the effort are two different things.

slides.title: Time-boxing a tricky task
slides.text: Giving yourself a set amount of time for one part of a problem, instead of an open-ended amount, keeps you from spending your whole time budget in a single place. For example, setting a firm 20-minute limit for research on a report keeps you from accidentally spending three hours there and having no time left to actually write it.

quiz.question: A new study method felt productive, but your test score didn't improve. What should you honestly check?
choices: Whether it actually solved the real problem
Only whether it felt fun to try
quiz.explanation: It's important to honestly check whether a solution actually worked, not just whether trying it felt productive. If a study method felt good but your score didn't improve, that mismatch matters more than how it felt.

quiz.question: You're stuck on a coding project after trying hard on your own. What's a smart move?
choices: Ask a teacher or search for help online
Never ask for help under any circumstances
quiz.explanation: Asking for help after genuinely trying on your own is a sign of good judgment, not failure. Asking a teacher or finding a forum post from someone who solved the same issue is a smart, efficient next step.

quiz.question: A group project fell behind schedule. What helps most afterward?
choices: Figuring out specifically where it slipped, like unclear roles
Just feeling bad about it and moving on
quiz.explanation: Looking back at exactly where a plan went wrong teaches you far more than simply feeling bad about it. Learning it fell behind because of unclear roles, not a missed deadline, tells you specifically what to fix next time.

quiz.question: You have a week to prepare for a debate. Why set rough time limits for research, practice, and rebuttals?
choices: Time limits only get in the way of good preparation
It keeps you from spending all your time on just one part
quiz.explanation: Setting rough time limits for each part keeps you from perfecting one piece while ignoring the rest. Without limits, it's easy to spend five days researching and have only one day left to actually practice.

quiz.question: Why decide before a school clean-up event that success means "at least 20 bags of trash collected"?
choices: It gives you an honest way to measure success afterward
Deciding this in advance ruins the event
quiz.explanation: Deciding upfront exactly what success looks like gives you an honest way to judge the results afterward. Without a clear measure decided in advance, it's easy to just guess based on how the day felt.

quiz.question: A lemonade stand made little money on a slow street corner. What's the smarter next move?
choices: Set up in the exact same spot again and hope for better luck
Move to a busier corner as a specific, intentional change
quiz.explanation: If a first attempt falls short, making one specific, intentional change is far more useful than repeating the same approach and hoping for a different result. Moving to a busier corner is a concrete change worth testing.

quiz.question: Why jot down a quick note like "homework right after school works better than after dinner"?
choices: It builds a habit of noticing useful patterns over time
Writing notes like this never actually helps
quiz.explanation: Jotting a quick note about what worked builds a habit of noticing your own patterns over time. A few small notes like this can eventually add up to genuinely useful personal rules.

quiz.question: After forgetting to charge a laptop before a presentation, which is more useful?
choices: Just resolving to "be more careful" next time
Making a concrete rule: "charge devices the night before, every time"
quiz.explanation: Turning a specific mistake into a concrete rule makes the lesson far more likely to actually stick. A rule like charging devices the night before is much more useful than vaguely resolving to "be more careful."

quiz.question: You prepare well for a tryout but still don't make the team. What's true here?
choices: The preparation was completely wasted
The effort was solid even though the outcome wasn't what you wanted
quiz.explanation: Sometimes you do everything right and still don't get the result you hoped for. Preparing seriously for a tryout and not making the team means the outcome and the effort are simply two separate things.

quiz.question: Why set a firm 20-minute limit for research on a report?
choices: It keeps research from eating all the time meant for writing
Time limits on research are never actually useful
quiz.explanation: Giving yourself a set amount of time for one part of a task, instead of leaving it open-ended, protects time for the other parts that also need it. A firm limit keeps research from swallowing the whole schedule.

slides.title: A structured framework: define, plan, execute, review
slides.text: Many effective problem solvers follow a loose structure: clearly define the problem, plan an approach, execute it, then review what actually happened. For example, tackling a group project might mean first defining exactly what's due, then planning who does what by when, then actually doing the work, then reviewing afterward whether the plan actually worked well for next time.

slides.title: Root cause analysis
slides.text: Instead of treating symptoms, root cause analysis asks 'why' repeatedly until you reach the actual underlying cause of a problem, not just its surface effects. For example, if you keep missing assignment deadlines, asking "why?" repeatedly might go: forgetting the due date → not writing it down → not having a consistent planner system — revealing that the real fix is a planning system, not just "trying harder to remember."

slides.title: Deciding under real constraints
slides.text: Real-world problems often come with limits — time, money, resources. Good problem solving works within those constraints instead of ignoring them. For example, planning a class fundraiser with only $20 of seed money and two weeks of prep time means the solution has to realistically fit those limits, not assume unlimited time and budget.

slides.title: Prioritizing which problem to solve first
slides.text: When facing multiple problems at once, deciding which one to tackle first — based on urgency and impact — is itself an important problem-solving skill. For example, if you're behind on a homework assignment due tomorrow and also want to reorganize your room, tackling the urgent, high-impact homework first is the smarter priority, even if reorganizing feels more appealing right now.

slides.title: First-principles thinking
slides.text: First-principles thinking means breaking a problem down to its most basic, undeniable facts and building a solution up from there, instead of just copying how it's usually done. For example, instead of assuming a fundraiser has to be a bake sale because that's tradition, first-principles thinking asks what you actually need — attention and small donations — and then considers any way to get those two things.

slides.title: The "5 Whys" technique
slides.text: A structured way to perform root cause analysis is asking "why" five times in a row, since the fifth answer is often far closer to the true root cause than the first. For example, "why did I fail the quiz?" leads to "didn't study enough," then "why?" leads to "started too late," then "why?" leads to "no fixed study time" — eventually revealing a scheduling problem, not a knowledge problem.

slides.title: Defining success before you start
slides.text: Deciding in advance exactly what a successful outcome looks like prevents quietly redefining "success" after the fact just to feel like you won. For example, deciding "improve my mile time by 30 seconds" before a training block begins gives you an honest, fixed way to judge the results later, rather than adjusting the bar afterward.

slides.title: Scoping the problem correctly
slides.text: A problem defined too broadly, like "fix my grades," is hard to act on, while one defined too narrowly, like "get one extra point on Tuesday's quiz," misses the bigger picture — good scoping finds a useful middle ground. For example, "raise my math grade this semester" is specific enough to plan around, without being so narrow that it misses the actual goal.

slides.title: Distinguishing symptoms from causes
slides.text: A symptom is the visible effect, while the cause is what's actually producing it underneath, and treating only the symptom never fixes the real problem. For example, a phone that runs slowly is a symptom — restarting it daily treats the symptom, but clearing out the too-many background apps causing it addresses the actual cause.

slides.title: Sequencing dependent problems
slides.text: Some problems must be solved before others even become solvable, so figuring out the right order matters as much as solving each piece. For example, it's not realistic to plan a road-trip budget before deciding on the route, since the route itself determines gas and lodging costs.

quiz.question: What are the four loose stages of a structured problem-solving framework?
choices: Define, plan, execute, review
Guess, hope, wait, forget
quiz.explanation: This four-stage structure keeps problem solving organized instead of chaotic: define the problem, plan an approach, execute it, then review what happened. For a group project, that means defining what's due, planning who does what, doing the work, then reviewing whether it worked.

quiz.question: You keep missing deadlines. Asking "why" repeatedly reveals the real issue is no planner system, not "forgetfulness." What is this called?
choices: Root cause analysis — finding the underlying cause, not just the symptom
Only ever addressing the most visible symptom
quiz.explanation: Root cause analysis means repeatedly asking "why" until you reach the actual underlying cause, instead of stopping at the first obvious answer. Missing deadlines might trace back to not having a consistent planner system, not just forgetfulness.

quiz.question: Why should real-world constraints (like a $20 budget and two weeks) be part of a fundraiser plan?
choices: Good solutions have to work within real limits
Constraints should always be ignored completely
quiz.explanation: Real-world problems almost always come with limits like time, money, or resources, and good problem solving works within them instead of pretending they don't exist. A $20 budget and two weeks shape what's actually realistic to plan.

quiz.question: Homework is due tomorrow and your room could also use reorganizing. What helps decide which to tackle first?
choices: Considering urgency and impact
Always picking whichever one is easiest, regardless of importance
quiz.explanation: When facing more than one problem at once, deciding which to tackle first based on urgency and impact is itself an important skill. Homework due tomorrow outranks reorganizing, even if reorganizing feels more appealing right now.

quiz.question: Instead of assuming a fundraiser must be a bake sale, you ask what you actually need — attention and donations — and consider any way to get them. What is this approach called?
choices: First-principles thinking
Iterating
quiz.explanation: First-principles thinking means breaking a problem down to its most basic facts and building a solution from there, instead of just copying tradition. It asks what you actually need, not what's usually done.

quiz.question: Asking "why did I fail the quiz" five times in a row eventually reveals a scheduling problem instead of a knowledge problem. What is this technique called?
choices: The "5 Whys" technique
First-principles thinking
quiz.explanation: The "5 Whys" technique means asking why five times in a row, since the fifth answer is usually much closer to the true root cause than the first. It's how "didn't study enough" eventually becomes "no fixed study time."

quiz.question: Why decide "improve my mile time by 30 seconds" before training even begins?
choices: It's more motivating to leave the goal undefined
It prevents quietly redefining success after the fact
quiz.explanation: Deciding in advance exactly what success looks like gives you a fixed, honest way to judge the results later. Without that upfront definition, it's tempting to quietly redefine "success" just to feel like you won.

quiz.question: Why is "raise my math grade this semester" better scoped than either "fix my grades" or "get one extra point Tuesday"?
choices: It finds a useful middle ground between too broad and too narrow
Extremely broad or extremely narrow problems are always easiest to solve
quiz.explanation: A problem scoped too broadly, like "fix my grades," is too vague to plan around, while one scoped too narrowly misses the bigger picture. "Raise my math grade this semester" is specific enough to plan real steps around without losing the goal.

quiz.question: A slow phone is restarted daily instead of having its background apps cleared out. What's the difference here?
choices: Restarting treats the symptom; clearing apps addresses the actual cause
Restarting and clearing apps address the exact same thing
quiz.explanation: A symptom is the visible effect you notice, while the cause is what's actually producing it underneath. Restarting a slow phone offers temporary relief, but clearing out the background apps causing the slowdown fixes the real problem.

quiz.question: Why decide on a road-trip route before planning its budget?
choices: The route determines costs like gas and lodging, so it must be decided first
Budgets and routes are always completely unrelated
quiz.explanation: Some problems have to be solved before others even become solvable, so the right order matters as much as solving each piece. The route itself determines costs like gas and lodging, so it comes first.

slides.title: Creative and lateral thinking
slides.text: Sometimes the best solution comes from approaching a problem sideways — questioning assumptions or combining unrelated ideas — rather than the most obvious direct approach. For example, if a school club is struggling to attract new members through the usual sign-up sheet, borrowing a completely different idea — like a fun demo event from an unrelated club that worked well — might solve it better than just posting more flyers.

slides.title: Collaborative problem solving
slides.text: Complex problems often benefit from multiple perspectives — dividing a big problem among a team can be far more effective than solving it entirely alone. For example, organizing a school event alone means one person handling logistics, marketing, and budget — but splitting those three areas among three people, each focusing on their strength, usually produces a much better result.

slides.title: Iterating toward a better solution
slides.text: Instead of expecting a perfect solution on the first try, iterating — improving a working-but-imperfect solution over several rounds — often produces the strongest result. For example, a first draft of a presentation might be rough, but reviewing and improving it two or three times — tightening the argument, fixing the slides — usually produces something far stronger than expecting perfection on the very first attempt.

slides.title: Combining multiple solutions
slides.text: Sometimes the strongest answer isn't picking just one option, but combining the best parts of several different approaches into one. For example, instead of choosing purely between studying alone or in a group, combining both — reviewing material alone first, then discussing tricky parts in a group — often works better than either approach used entirely on its own.

slides.title: Communicating your solution
slides.text: A good solution can fail simply because it wasn't explained clearly to the people who need to understand or approve it. For example, pitching a new club schedule to a teacher works better when you clearly state the problem, your proposed fix, and why it benefits everyone — not just handing over a vague idea and hoping they fill in the reasoning.

slides.title: Dividing roles by strength, not fairness
slides.text: When splitting a group problem, assigning tasks based on who's strongest at each part, rather than splitting everything evenly, usually produces a better final result, even if the split looks uneven on paper. For example, letting the strongest writer handle the script and the strongest designer handle the visuals produces a stronger group project than insisting everyone do a little of everything.

slides.title: Building on someone else's idea
slides.text: In group problem-solving, improving a teammate's half-formed idea often works better than scrapping it for a completely different one — refining tends to beat restarting. For example, if a teammate suggests a rough theme for a fundraiser, sharpening that idea together usually gets further than arguing for an entirely separate concept from scratch.

slides.title: Borrowing solutions from unrelated fields
slides.text: Lateral thinking often means noticing that a solution from a completely different area applies here too, not just staring harder at the problem itself. For example, using a restaurant's "text you when your table's ready" idea to manage sign-ups for a crowded school club meeting solves a scheduling problem by borrowing from an unrelated industry.

slides.title: Explaining the "why," not just the "what"
slides.text: When pitching a solution to someone with the power to approve it, like a teacher or a parent, explaining the reasoning behind the choice is usually more persuasive than just stating the plan itself. For example, explaining why a later club meeting time fits more students' schedules is more convincing than simply asking for the time to be changed.

slides.title: Getting feedback before the final version
slides.text: Sharing an early draft of a solution and asking specifically what's confusing or weak produces better results than polishing alone in isolation and hoping it lands. For example, showing a rough draft of a presentation to a friend and asking "what part is confusing?" catches problems that are hard to see after staring at your own work for hours.

quiz.question: A club borrows an idea from an unrelated club to attract new members, instead of just posting more flyers. What does this show?
choices: Lateral thinking — approaching a problem sideways
Only ever using the most obvious, direct approach
quiz.explanation: Lateral thinking means approaching a problem sideways — questioning assumptions or borrowing ideas from elsewhere — instead of only trying the obvious direct approach. Borrowing a fun demo event idea from another club is one example.

quiz.question: Organizing a school event alone means handling logistics, marketing, and budget all yourself. What usually produces a better result?
choices: Splitting those three areas among three people, each using their strength
Insisting one person handle everything alone
quiz.explanation: Complex problems often benefit from multiple perspectives, since dividing a big problem among a team can be far more effective than one person alone. Splitting logistics, marketing, and budget among three people playing to their strengths usually works better.

quiz.question: A rough presentation draft is improved over two or three rounds instead of expected to be perfect immediately. What is this called?
choices: Iterating — improving a working-but-imperfect solution over rounds
Expecting the very first attempt to be flawless
quiz.explanation: Iterating means improving a working-but-imperfect solution over several rounds instead of expecting perfection on the first try. A rough draft tightened two or three times usually ends up far stronger than a rushed final attempt.

quiz.question: Studying alone first, then discussing tricky parts in a group, combines two approaches. What can this produce?
choices: A stronger answer than picking just one option
Always rejecting every approach except one
quiz.explanation: Sometimes the strongest answer isn't one single approach but a combination of the best parts of several. Reviewing alone first and then discussing tricky parts in a group often beats relying entirely on either method alone.

quiz.question: Why might a good solution fail even if the idea itself is solid?
choices: It wasn't clearly explained to the people who need to approve it
Good ideas can never fail for any reason
quiz.explanation: A good solution can fail simply because it was never clearly explained to the people who need to understand or approve it. Stating the problem, the fix, and why it helps matters as much as the idea itself.

quiz.question: Why let the strongest writer handle the script and the strongest designer handle the visuals, instead of splitting every task evenly?
choices: It usually produces a better final result even if the split looks uneven
Every task should always be split perfectly evenly no matter what
quiz.explanation: Assigning tasks based on who's strongest at each part, instead of splitting everything evenly, usually produces a better result even though the split looks uneven on paper. The best writer on script beats everyone doing a little of everything.

quiz.question: A teammate suggests a rough fundraiser theme. What usually works better than proposing a totally different idea?
choices: Scrapping it immediately for something unrelated
Sharpening and building on that half-formed idea together
quiz.explanation: In group problem-solving, improving a teammate's half-formed idea usually works better than scrapping it entirely, since refining tends to beat restarting. Sharpening a rough theme together often gets further than arguing for something completely separate.

quiz.question: Using a restaurant's "text you when your table's ready" idea to manage sign-ups for a crowded club meeting is an example of what?
choices: Borrowing a solution from a completely unrelated field
Sticking strictly to solutions already used in that same field
quiz.explanation: Lateral thinking often means noticing that a solution from a completely different field applies here too, instead of only staring harder at the problem. Borrowing the restaurant's text alert idea solves the club's scheduling problem.

quiz.question: When pitching a later club meeting time to a teacher, what's usually more persuasive than just stating the request?
choices: Explaining why it fits more students' schedules
Leaving out the reasoning and just stating the plan
quiz.explanation: When pitching a solution to someone with the power to approve it, explaining the reasoning behind the choice is usually more persuasive than just stating the plan. Saying why a later time fits more schedules works better than a bare request.

quiz.question: Why show a rough draft to a friend and ask "what part is confusing?" before finishing it?
choices: It catches problems that are hard to see after staring at your own work for hours
Feedback on an unfinished draft is always a waste of time
quiz.explanation: Sharing an early draft and specifically asking what's confusing usually produces better results than polishing alone in isolation. It catches problems that are nearly impossible to see after staring at your own work for hours.

slides.title: Treating failure as data
slides.text: A failed attempt isn't just a setback — it's information about what doesn't work, which narrows down what might work next. For example, if your first attempt at a part-time job application gets rejected, treating that as data — maybe your resume needs work, or you should apply to more places — is more useful than treating it as proof you're not employable.

slides.title: Problems with no perfect answer
slides.text: Some real problems don't have one clearly best solution — every option involves trade-offs. Choosing the option with the best overall balance is often the most realistic goal. For example, choosing between two part-time job offers might mean one pays more but has worse hours, while the other pays less but fits your schedule better — there's no perfect answer, just the best overall balance for your situation.

slides.title: Watching out for your own bias
slides.text: Confirmation bias — the tendency to notice evidence that supports what you already believe, while ignoring evidence that doesn't — can quietly steer you toward the wrong solution. For example, if you're convinced a friend group is the reason your grades dropped, you might notice every distracting hangout but overlook the nights you stayed up late for other reasons, missing the real cause.

slides.title: Weighing the risk before committing
slides.text: Before committing fully to a solution, it's worth asking what could go wrong and how bad that would actually be — this is basic risk assessment. For example, before investing your entire savings into a resale side-business, weighing the realistic chance of losing that money against the safer option of starting with just a fraction of it is a genuinely mature problem-solving step.

slides.title: Sunk cost fallacy
slides.text: Continuing to pour time or money into a failing plan just because a lot has already been invested in it is called the sunk cost fallacy — a rational decision should weigh what happens next, not what's already spent. For example, finishing a club project that clearly isn't working just because months were already put into it can waste even more time than cutting losses and stopping now.

slides.title: Cooling off before a big decision
slides.text: For a decision with real consequences, deliberately waiting a day before finalizing it can prevent an emotional, in-the-moment choice that gets regretted later. For example, waiting until the next day to decide whether to quit a team, instead of deciding right after a frustrating loss, usually leads to a clearer-headed choice.

slides.title: Estimating probability, not just possibility
slides.text: Almost anything is technically "possible," but good risk assessment asks how likely something actually is, not just whether it could theoretically happen. For example, worrying equally about a common risk, like forgetting a permission slip, and a rare one, like a citywide event cancellation, leads to spending energy in the wrong place.

slides.title: Anchoring bias
slides.text: The first number or idea encountered tends to unfairly influence judgment of everything that comes after it, even when that first piece of information wasn't especially reliable. For example, assuming a certain price is fair for a used bike just because the first listing seen happened to be expensive can lead to overpaying later without realizing it.

slides.title: Checking your own blind spots
slides.text: Because it's genuinely hard to spot your own biases, asking someone with a different perspective to review a big decision can reveal a blind spot that would otherwise go unnoticed. For example, a friend outside a friend group's dynamics might notice a plan is unfair to one member in a way the friend group itself completely missed.

slides.title: Considering second-order effects
slides.text: Beyond the immediate result, a good solution also considers what happens next because of it, not just whether it solves the first problem. For example, a strict new team rule might solve one immediate problem but cause several teammates to quit — a second-order effect worth predicting before the rule is put in place.

quiz.question: A job application gets rejected. How should that be treated?
choices: As data that narrows down what might work next
As proof that you're unemployable
quiz.explanation: A failed attempt isn't just a setback — it's actual information about what doesn't work, which narrows down what might work better next. A rejection might mean your resume needs revising, which is more useful than treating it as proof you're unemployable.

quiz.question: Two job offers each have trade-offs (better pay vs. better hours). What is realistic here?
choices: Choosing the option with the best overall balance of trade-offs
Refusing to decide until a perfect option appears
quiz.explanation: Some real problems don't have one clearly perfect answer, since every option involves trade-offs, so choosing the best overall balance is the realistic goal. Between better pay and better hours, there's no flawless choice — just the best fit for you.

quiz.question: You're sure a friend group caused your grades to drop, and you keep noticing evidence that fits that idea while ignoring other explanations. What is this called?
choices: Confirmation bias
Root cause analysis
quiz.explanation: Confirmation bias is the tendency to notice evidence that supports what you already believe while ignoring evidence that doesn't. Noticing every distracting hangout while overlooking late nights caused by something else is a classic example.

quiz.question: Before investing your entire savings into a resale side-business, what is the mature problem-solving step?
choices: Weighing the realistic chance of loss against starting with just a fraction of the money
Investing everything at once without considering what could go wrong
quiz.explanation: Basic risk assessment means asking what could realistically go wrong and how bad that outcome would actually be before committing fully. Weighing the chance of losing everything against starting small is a genuinely mature step.

quiz.question: A club project clearly isn't working, but months have already gone into it. What is it called to keep going anyway just because of that past investment?
choices: The sunk cost fallacy
Root cause analysis
quiz.explanation: The sunk cost fallacy is continuing to pour time or money into a failing plan just because a lot has already been invested, rather than weighing what happens next. Finishing a doomed project just because of past effort can waste even more time.

quiz.question: Why wait a day before deciding whether to quit a team, instead of deciding right after a frustrating loss?
choices: Waiting can prevent an emotional decision that gets regretted later
Decisions made immediately after strong emotions are always the clearest
quiz.explanation: For a decision with real consequences, deliberately waiting a day before finalizing it can prevent an emotional, in-the-moment choice you later regret. Deciding the day after a loss usually leads to a clearer-headed decision.

quiz.question: Why is worrying equally about a common risk and a rare one a mistake?
choices: Good risk assessment estimates how likely something actually is, not just whether it's possible
Every possible risk deserves exactly equal amounts of worry
quiz.explanation: Almost anything is technically possible, but good risk assessment asks how likely something actually is, not just whether it could happen. Worrying equally about a common risk and a rare one wastes energy in the wrong place.

quiz.question: Seeing an expensive first bike listing makes every other price seem reasonable by comparison. What is this called?
choices: Anchoring bias
Sunk cost fallacy
quiz.explanation: Anchoring bias is the tendency for the first number or idea you encounter to unfairly influence how you judge everything after it, even if that first piece of information wasn't reliable. An expensive first listing can make later prices seem falsely reasonable.

quiz.question: Why might a friend outside a friend group notice a plan is unfair to one member when the group itself missed it?
choices: An outside perspective can reveal a blind spot you can't see on your own
People inside a situation always see it more clearly than outsiders
quiz.explanation: Because it's genuinely hard to notice your own biases, asking someone with a different perspective to review a decision can reveal a blind spot you'd otherwise miss. An outsider isn't tangled up in the group's dynamics.

quiz.question: A strict new team rule solves one problem but causes several teammates to quit. What is this an example of?
choices: A second-order effect worth predicting in advance
Something that could never have been predicted
quiz.explanation: Beyond the immediate result, a good solution also considers what happens next because of it, not just whether it fixes the first problem. A rule that solves one issue but drives teammates to quit is a second-order effect worth predicting.
